extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing literary writers, critics, and educated readers
extracted.subtask_description: Critical, essayistic guidance about the habits, temperament, social conditions, and bodily constitution that favor producing valuable literature; evaluates professional authorship vs. combining writing with other employment. Useful for writers considering how to organize life and work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical constitution and endurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who produce sustained, 'weighty' literary work need a bodily constitution able to support Herculean endurance and continuity — likened to horses or 'Centaurs'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author cites Goethe and Sir Walter Scott as examples; claims few literary geniuses possess great toughness of fibre. A strong and active body is a condition for sustained literary output; without such constitution continuous composition may wear a man out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and compass of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius should be 'not merely powerful, but distinguished for variety and compass of power.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variety of mind complements physical endurance to enable large-scale literary achievement; mental breadth is explicitly valued alongside force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from sole literary livelihood
rubrics_metrics.description: The best and most valuable literary works are often produced by men who did not depend on literary performance for their livelihood or who had regular employment besides writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Jeremy Taylor, Locke, Newton, Berkeley, Hume, Hartley, Leibnitz, Milton. Dependence on literature for bread creates anxiety that weakens quality; having another calling can concentrate force and improve output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of composing mechanically/daily
rubrics_metrics.description: Composing every day and all day — mechanical, regular composition — tends to foster literary growth of inferior value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The power of composing continuously may produce extensive works but not necessarily the most exquisite or valuable ones; resistance and some restraint can concentrate creative force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between literary seclusion and public engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Being entirely shut up in study (e.g., 'shut up in a fortress' with books) is not necessarily the best preparation for writing well; public labor and engagement can qualify a writer in beneficial ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Herder's wish for seclusion is cited but questioned — life and public duties may enrich literature; the essay argues that those entering public arenas can be better qualified than hermits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic arrangements and quiet companionship
rubrics_metrics.description: A domestic life allowing 'social silence' and a wife who can be happily occupied while the husband pursues study is favorable; quiet evenings where spouse is present but not demanding conversation are valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge's evening-plan (quiet study with wife's presence) is defended: a wife need not be constantly engaged in talk; children should be put to bed so grown persons can work in the evening. Examples: Wieland's contentment from knowing his wife was nearby.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing family responsibilities for literary work
rubrics_metrics.description: Household demands and noisy children can hinder evening study; practical arrangements (nursery, schooling, sisters/governesses) are part of making literary life possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not an attack on domestic life but a practical observation: many professional men cannot realize ideal quiet because their profession or society's demands occupy their time; younger children should be sheltered to allow evening study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperamental sensitivity vs. practical resilience
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive nervous delicacy and morbid sensitiveness can unfit a man for continuous literary labour; temperament must be robust enough to endure anxiety and hardship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Herder's hypochondria is used as an example: doubling literary labor under anxiety would not have improved him. By contrast, figures like Jean Paul (who sometimes grew stronger under hardship) are exceptional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poverty: possible stimulant but often narcotic
rubrics_metrics.description: While poverty may stimulate some persons' energies, for the majority of sensitive men it acts as a narcotic that dulls creative powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jean Paul's experience is contrasted with many who are crushed by want; poverty can produce varied outcomes — purification and invincibility in a few, dulness or despair in many.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical prudence about money matters
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Indifference to money matters' may be gentlemanly but often amounts to incoherence or madness; some practical concern for means is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay warns against romanticizing indifference to money; financial neglect can harm the writer's life and work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of varied life-experience and occupation
rubrics_metrics.description: Literature 'draws its life from all that enlivens and invigorates the man'; engagement in other duties can supply material and vigor for literary creation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular employment or public duties supply resistance and experiences that enrich literature. Works produced 'in addition to regular employment' can be of high value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding personal invective in literary dispute
rubrics_metrics.description: When criticizing or contesting literary offences confine oneself to describing the literary offences themselves rather than attacking personal character, motives, or feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author praises restraint: exposing literary wrongs is proper, but descending into personal caricature or insinuation is improper; better to describe offences and avoid uncharitable speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to write well in prime and choose fitting vehicle
rubrics_metrics.description: It is crucial that writers can write genially while their intellect is in its prime, and then choose the worthiest vehicle for their peculiar powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should be free to select forms that suit their strengths; the end goal is to 'array their temple with the Muses' diadem' — quality over sheer quantity or continuous output.
